claim: Zionism is a colonial project that stole the land.

answer: For about 400 years the land was Ottoman. It was never one province: the south was the district of Jerusalem, the north was split between the provinces of Beirut and Syria, and none was called Palestine. British forces took Jerusalem in December 1917. The Balfour Declaration (November 1917) favoured a Jewish national home and said nothing should prejudice the 'civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities', without mentioning their political rights. The League of Nations confirmed a British Mandate in 1922 that recited the Jewish people's historical connection to the land, and Transjordan was excluded from the national-home clauses. Britain's 1939 White Paper then limited Jewish immigration. In 1915 Britain's High Commissioner in Egypt offered Arab independence except for some districts of Syria; whether that left Palestine out is disputed. In the years these facts cover, sovereignty lay with the Ottoman Empire and then with Britain as Mandatory.

facts.text: Under Ottoman rule no province was named Palestine. The south was the independent sanjak (Mutasarrifate) of Jerusalem, answering directly to Istanbul; the north belonged to the vilayet of Beirut (the sanjaks of Acre and Nablus) and, before 1888, to the vilayet of Syria (Damascus).

contested.text: Whether McMahon's 1915 promise covered Palestine is disputed. The British government's 1939 White Paper held that the whole of Palestine west of the Jordan was excluded from the pledge. But the 1939 committee report records that the British representatives themselves told the Arab side that its case 'has greater force than has appeared hitherto' and that the language of exclusion was 'not so specific and unmistakable as it was thought to be at the time', while still maintaining that on a proper construction Palestine was excluded. The Arab representatives argued that Palestine was in fact and in intention included in the area of promised Arab independence, and that reading 'district' as 'vilayet' was untenable. A 2011 Commonweal review of a book by Jonathan Schneer notes it has been argued that the Arabic translation led Hussein to read 'districts' more widely; that line is a reviewer's summary, not a historian's own words. Historians still differ; this card reports the dispute, not a verdict.

contested.text: Whether Britain's wartime promises were consistent is contested. The Imperial War Museums say Britain had already promised Palestine to the Arabs as an independent state and promised France an internationally administered zone before it signed the Balfour Declaration. Israel's Foreign Ministry reads the Declaration, and its inclusion in the Mandate, as international recognition of the Jewish people's right to self-determination in its historical homeland.

not_claimed: This card does not say Palestine was empty or that no people with a claim lived there before 1917; chapter 2's population card gives the counts.
It does not say the Balfour Declaration or the Mandate settled who owned the land or created a right of the Jewish people over the Arabs of Palestine.
It does not say Britain kept its promises to either side.
It does not say the White Paper stopped Jewish immigration entirely; it set a quota.

It was never one province: the south was the district of Jerusalem, the north was split between the provinces of Beirut and Syria, and none was called Palestine.

The Balfour Declaration (November 1917) favoured a Jewish national home and said nothing should prejudice the 'civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities', without mentioning their political rights.

Britain's 1939 White Paper then limited Jewish immigration.

skeptic.notes: Read 2+ sources per fact (all 10) with the paragraph around each quote. Quotes are accurate. [must-fix] contested[0] said the British 1939 review 'held' Palestine was excluded and left out that the same report records the British delegation conceding the Arab case had 'greater force' and the exclusion language was 'not so specific and unmistakable'; a Palestinian historian would call that minimising. I added the concession (from the report already cited). [must-fix] The card has no fact on Mandate Article 6 (facilitate Jewish immigration, close settlement on State and waste lands) or Article 4 (Jewish Agency as public body); without them 'ruled by empires, not Zionists' is one-sided. Needs new fact(s) from the Avalon text: cannot be added by the reviewer. [must-fix] Facts 5-7: the three hosts (Avalon, Fordham, UNISPAL) reproduce one document, so each is one source for what the Mandate says; I counted it as one strong primary source, not three. Fact 5's preamble clause is read in none of the quotes except Avalon's. [should-fix] Fact 8: the quote was cut so that it read as exclusion from 'the Articles of the Mandate'; I extended it to the clause the report actually states. Palquest and LOC pages were unreadable (403). [should-fix] Fact 9: the FRUS page is a US memorandum summarising the White Paper, and fact 4's FRUS page is a US despatch quoting The Times; both relabelled as summaries. Fact 4 third source is a 2011 book review, now labelled. [should-fix] 'heard' (Khalidi) carries the 'colonial' half of the claim only; nothing on the card answers 'stole the land'. [nit] Answer quoted 'existing non-Jewish communities' as if the promise covered all rights; reworded to 'civil and religious'. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, the missing Art. 6 and the minimised British concession; Israeli side, none found (the Mandate preamble and Art. 2 are quoted in full).

citer.notes: Split the answer into 8 sentences, each tied to facts. Removed: 'So the land was ruled by empires, not Zionists, until 1948' (no fact covers 1948 and Art. 4 gives the Jewish Agency a role the card does not show); replaced by a sentence limited to Ottoman then British sovereignty (facts 1, 5, 6). Reworded the Balfour sentence from 'the rights' to 'civil and religious rights' and added the no-political-rights point (fact 3). Replaced 'Whether Britain had earlier promised Palestine to the Arabs is disputed' with the McMahon offer it rests on (fact 4); the dispute itself lives in contested. Verdict covers the answer's tie to the facts; the weaknesses above are in the facts and the missing Art. 6.
